post.description: Helps Pennsylvania households pay for home heating with a once-a-season grant (LIHEAP Cash, 2026-27 season).

Eligible.description: A one-person household in Pennsylvania with $23,940 a year, exactly 150% of the 2026 poverty guideline. It pays its own heating bill, has a U.S. citizen, and has not received Cash this season, so it is eligible.

Heat in income-based rent.description: A renter whose heat is included in rent set as a share of income. LIHEAP Cash does not cover heat paid through income-based rent, so the household is not eligible.

Income over limit.description: A household of four with $49,501 a year, $1 over the 150% limit of $49,500. The income check fails, so the household is not eligible.

eligible.body:
Apply online through COMPASS during the season, which runs from November 2, 2026 to April 23, 2027. You can also apply at your County Assistance Office.

- Have proof of income for everyone in the household, for the month before you apply or for the past 12 months.
- Have a recent heating bill, or a statement from your landlord if heat is part of your rent.
- Apply early. The season can close before April if the money runs out.

For help, call the LIHEAP hotline at 1-866-857-7095 (TTY 711).

ineligible.note: If you have a heating emergency, such as a shutoff notice or running out of fuel, you may still qualify for LIHEAP Crisis. Call the LIHEAP hotline at 1-866-857-7095.

administeredBy.name: Pennsylvania Department of Human Services, through the County Assistance Offices

checks.rationale: LIHEAP Cash is for households that permanently live in Pennsylvania (601.31(3)).
Household income must be equal to or less than 150% of the federal poverty guidelines (601.81 to 601.84).
The household must be responsible for its primary heating costs. Households whose heat is included in rent based on their income are not eligible (601.31(2)).
Someone in the household must be a U.S. citizen or a lawfully admitted non-citizen (601.31(4)).
A household can receive one Cash grant per season (601.43).

x-bdt-reference.explanation: LIHEAP Cash is a grant that helps households pay for home heating during the winter season. This benefit checks the main rules for the 2026-27 season: the household lives in Pennsylvania, its income is at or below 150% of the federal poverty guidelines, it is responsible for its primary heating costs, someone in it is a U.S. citizen or lawfully admitted non-citizen, and it has not already received a Cash grant this season.

implementationNotes.text: Season dates are documentation only: the rules do not check the screening date. Dated parameters (https://github.com/CodeForPhilly/benefit-decision-toolkit/issues/568) and Periods (https://github.com/CodeForPhilly/benefit-decision-toolkit/issues/550) would let the season and the poverty guideline year follow the screening date.
householdSize and householdIncome are used as given. The screener has to apply LIHEAP's rules for whose income counts (601.81 to 601.84) and who is left out of household size (601.41(1)).

limitations: Living arrangements that make a household ineligible are not checked: temporary stays, institutions, dorms, fraternity or sorority houses, boarding homes, incarceration, and fleeing felons.
Heating equipment that is not installed or operating to code is not checked, and neither are the rules for recreational vehicles and home businesses.
Household size and income are taken as given. LIHEAP leaves ineligible non-citizens, and people who already got Cash in another household, out of household size but still counts their income.
The applicant may choose the prior month or the prior 12 months as the income period. The screener does not compare the two.
DHS may change the season dates, and the funds can run out before the season closes.
Income limits change each February, when DHS adopts the new federal poverty guidelines.

eligible.body:
Apply through the Philadelphia Tax Center. You do not need an online account. You can also apply by phone or use the paper application on the program page.

- Apply by December 1. Applying by October 1 helps put the exemption on your next bill.
- If a previous owner is still listed, call the hotline or use the paper application.
- After approval, you usually do not need to apply again unless your deed changes.

ineligible.note: If your name is not on the deed, you may still qualify for a conditional Homestead Exemption. Check the program page for the paper application and supporting documents.

eligible.body:
Use the Philadelphia Tax Center to find your property, open its OPA number, and choose the real estate assistance application. The program page also has a paper application.

- Include proof of income.
- Compare LOOP and Homestead savings before switching: you cannot receive both at once. Request Homestead removal with your LOOP application if needed.
- Applications are accepted throughout the year. Apply by September 30 for the benefit to apply to that year's bill.

ineligible.note: Receiving the Homestead Exemption does not stop you from applying for LOOP, but you must request Homestead removal when applying. Use the City's property tax calculator to compare the programs first.

Apply through the Philadelphia Tax Center using the combined real estate assistance application. You do not need an online account. The program page also explains how to apply by mail or in person.

Apply through the Philadelphia Tax Center using the combined real estate assistance application, or mail the paper application from the program page.

x-bdt-reference.explanation: Passes when the screener answer says someone in the household is a U.S. citizen or a lawfully admitted non-citizen, such as a lawful permanent resident, refugee, asylee, or someone paroled for at least one year. post.description: Checks that annual household income is at or below a percentage of the HHS poverty guidelines for the household's size.

One person at 150 percent.description: A one-person household with $23,940 a year is exactly at 150% of the 2026 poverty guideline, which matches PA LIHEAP's published limit, so the check passes.

One person over 150 percent.description: A one-person household with one cent more than $23,940 a year is over 150% of the 2026 guideline, so the check fails.

x-bdt-reference.explanation: Finds the HHS poverty guideline for the household's size, multiplies it by the given percent, and passes when annual household income is equal to or less than the result. For 2026 the guideline is $15,960 for one person plus $5,680 for each additional person, so 150% is $23,940 for one person plus $8,520 for each additional person. Returns no result when income or household size is missing or invalid, or when the guideline year is not available.

implementationNotes.text: The 2026 values were derived from PA LIHEAP's published 150% table ($23,940 for one person, plus $8,520 for each additional person). Add each new year to the guidelines list when HHS publishes it in January.

limitations: Only the 2026 guidelines are available. Any other guideline year returns no result.
Uses the guidelines for the 48 contiguous states and DC, not those for Alaska or Hawaii.
Takes household income and size as given. It does not decide whose income counts, which income is excluded, or how pay is annualized.
Does not round the limit. A program that publishes rounded limits may differ by a few dollars.

post.description: Checks that the household pays for its primary heat, and not through income-based rent that includes heat.

Heat in income-based rent.description: The household's heat is included in rent set as a share of its income, so the check fails even though the household says it pays for heat.

Pass.description: The household pays its own heating bill and its heat is not part of income-based rent, so the check passes.

x-bdt-reference.explanation: Passes when the household is responsible for the cost of its primary heat, paid directly to a fuel or utility company or as an undesignated part of its rent, and its heat is not included in rent that is set as a share of its income or by its source of income. Fails when either answer rules the household out, and returns no result when an answer needed to decide is missing.
limitations: Does not check that the heating equipment is installed and operating to code.
Does not apply the rules for recreational vehicles or homes used for a business.
Relies on the screener answers to say what the primary heat is. Supplemental heat alone does not count.
A renter whose rent includes a designated heat portion counts as paying for heat, so the screener question has to cover that case.
